title: Where Did the Idea of Progress Come From?

keyTerms.d: “The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice” — Martin Luther King Jr.’s favourite line, a later compression of the abolitionist minister Theodore Parker (1853). Parker was more honest than the compression: “I cannot calculate the curve and complete the figure by the experience of sight; I can divine it by conscience. But from what I see I am sure it bends towards justice.” The image says history is going somewhere, that cruelties once thought normal can be named as evils and left behind — and in its original form it was a claim of faith, not of sight: the arc bends because Someone is bending it.

The oldest and most widespread picture of time is not a line but a circle. The Stoics taught that the cosmos passes through vast cycles, each ending in a universal fire and beginning again — and that when it begins again it repeats exactly: the same Socrates marries the same wife and is tried by the same accusers, endlessly, without remainder. On such a view nothing is ever finally gained or lost, because everything comes round again; the goddess Fortune turned her wheel, and the only wisdom was to expect the turn. There was no destination toward which the whole was moving, because there was no whole that moved.

The other dominant ancient picture: a slope running downhill. The Greek poet Hesiod (c. 700 BC) told of humanity beginning in a Golden Age, living like gods free of toil, then descending through a Silver race, a Bronze, the heroes, and finally the Iron race — his own — doomed to labour and grief and destined to grow worse until the gods abandoned it. The arrow, if there is one, points down. Where the golden age lies behind you, the task of the wise is not reform but memory: to recover what has been lost, not to build what has never been.

keyTerms.t: The judged line — the biblical arrow
keyTerms.d: What the ancient world lacked, the Hebrew Scriptures supplied: a story that runs in a straight line and is going somewhere — creation, a call to Abraham, a rescue from slavery in Egypt, a journey to a promised land, prophets who summon the nation back to its covenant, and a promised kingdom in which the wrongs of history are finally set right. Crucially, that road is judged — measured against a standard that lies ahead of it rather than behind. The prophets do not tell Israel to return to a golden age; they hold up a future in which justice arrives and indict the present for falling short of it (“let justice roll down like waters,” Amos; swords beaten into plowshares, Isaiah).

The contested scholarly claim, framed by Karl Löwith, that the modern philosophy of progress is a secularized form of biblical eschatology — Judeo-Christian hope in worldly dress. Hans Blumenberg replied that the idea of progress grows from within history, out of the open-ended experience of science and modern self-assertion, not from any borrowed eschatology; Robert Nisbet, unlike Löwith, credited the Greeks and Romans with real ideas of progress of their own. This essay does not endorse the stronger secularization thesis. What is not seriously disputed is narrower, and enough: the biblical narrative gave the West a distinctive and load-bearing picture of time as a line with a destination.

An arc has to bend toward something. A measurement of where we have gone cannot, by itself, tell us which direction counts as forward; for that you need a fixed point standing above history to be measured against — a standard the story cannot generate purely from within itself. Parker could name it: a justice fixed by conscience, which for him meant fixed by God. The confidence that history bends toward justice was born believing in that fixed point, and has not obviously found a replacement for it. (Whether a secular account can supply such a ground is the question of a companion essay, not this one; the point here is only historical.)

When the twentieth century recoiled from its own worst chapters, it reached backward for a footing it could no longer supply from within. The framers of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights did not deduce dignity from progress or from nature; they asserted it in their first line as “inherent,” and named in their second the “barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind.” It states, with magnificent clarity, what we must never do again; it says far less, from its own resources, about why. Jacques Maritain recorded the telling condition on which champions of opposed ideologies agreed a list of rights: “no one asks us why.”

derive.q: Step outside the modern West and the confidence that history improves largely evaporates: the oldest pictures of time are the wheel and the downhill slope. So the assumption that time’s direction is up is…?
derive.ans: not a human universal but an inheritance
derive.why: That assumption is not a human universal. It is not what most people who have ever lived believed. The idea that a society could look at its own past, judge it wanting, and set out deliberately to be better — that history is a story with a plot, headed toward a goal — is a specific and unusual conviction, not common sense.

derive.q: The prophets do not summon Israel back to a golden age; they hold up a future justice and indict the present for falling short of it. So the biblical road is not just a line but a line that is…?
derive.ans: judged — measured against a standard that lies ahead
derive.why: Crucially, that road is judged — measured against a standard that lies ahead of it rather than behind. The prophets do not tell Israel to return to a golden age; they hold up a future in which justice arrives, and indict the present for falling short of it. Here is a moral universe with an arc, and the arc bends because Someone is bending it.

derive.q: Steven Pinker, a thoroughgoing atheist, explains the retreat of the death penalty by writing that it has made it “seem as if there really is a mysterious arc bending toward justice.” That borrowing shows…?
derive.ans: the shape of the hope survives even when its root is let go — not that the root is real
derive.why: That is not a dead idiom; it is Parker’s image and King’s — and Parker’s arc bent, he said, because God was bending it. It is simply what happens when you keep the fruit and let go of the root: the shape of the hope remains, its origin forgotten. The argument rests not on the worn idioms (swords into plowshares, “life is sacred”) but on this single direct echo of the Parker–King arc.

derive.q: An arc has to bend toward something, and a measurement of where we have gone cannot by itself tell us which direction counts as forward. So the confidence that history bends toward justice still needs…?
derive.ans: a fixed point standing above history
derive.why: For that you need a fixed point standing above history to be measured against — a standard the story cannot generate purely from within itself. The confidence that history bends toward justice was born believing in that fixed point, and has not obviously found a replacement for it.

derive.q: Grant the whole genealogy — the hope’s roots really are biblical. Does that, by itself, prove Christianity is true?
derive.ans: no — roots are not proof; the case rests above all on the resurrection
derive.why: On its own it is no proof that Christianity is true. That a conviction has biblical roots tells you where it came from, not whether the faith that carried it is right about God; a tradition can seed a good idea and still be mistaken in its central claims. The case for the faith’s truth is made elsewhere in this Library, resting above all on the resurrection.

honestState.p1: What this argument establishes is bounded, and the essay keeps it in its lane. It is a genealogy: it traces where a load-bearing modern conviction — that history bends toward justice and the future can be deliberately made better than the past — came from, and it stops there. It shows the belief is not a human universal but an inheritance: the dominant ancient pictures of time were the wheel and the downhill slope, and the line with a judged destination came into the West through the biblical narrative, a shape even committed secularists still reach for. What it does not do, on its own, is prove that Christianity is true; roots are not proof.
honestState.fairness: The scholarship is reported, not flattened. Robert Nisbet is conceded his point that the Greeks and Romans had real ideas of progress of their own — the claim here is only that they lacked the further picture of history as a judged whole headed toward a goal. Karl Löwith’s strong secularization thesis (progress as secularized biblical eschatology) is named as contested, with Hans Blumenberg’s reply that progress grows from within history given in full; the essay follows only the narrower, shared claim and does not endorse Löwith. The Pinker borrowing is deliberately not overclaimed: two of the echoes (swords into plowshares, “life is sacred”) are worn idioms little should be made of on their own, and the point rests on the single direct echo of the Parker–King “arc.” Parker himself was a radical Unitarian who rejected much of historic Christian doctrine — a reminder that the argument needs no one to have been orthodox.
honestState.verdict: So the modern idea of progress is, in large part, the biblical arrow with the source filed off: the shape of the hope remains, its origin forgotten. The honest tension is narrower than a proof — an arc has to bend toward something, and a record of where we have gone cannot by itself tell us which direction counts as forward, so the confidence is living on inherited capital and owes an account of the fixed point it still assumes. Two limits hold the claim in place: on its own it is no proof that Christianity is true, and Christians have repeatedly stood on the wrong side of the very reforms this hope demands. The point is genealogical, not congratulatory. That even confident atheists keep the hope after discarding the God who grounded it is a small thread worth weighing, though never a proof — the case for the faith’s truth rests elsewhere, above all on the resurrection.

order: The belief that history bends toward justice and the future can be deliberately made better than the past is not a human universal; the dominant ancient pictures of time were the wheel and the downhill slope, and the biblical narrative gave the West its distinctive picture of time as a judged line heading toward a goal.

That confidence still depends on a fixed point above history to say which direction counts as forward — a record of where we have gone cannot supply it — and even committed secularists reach for the biblical arrow’s shape while its source is filed off.

Therefore the modern idea of progress is, in large part, a biblical inheritance still leaning on the fixed point it was given — which shows where the hope came from, not, by itself, that Christianity is true.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The belief that history has a direction — that it bends toward justice and the future can be deliberately made better than the past — is not a human universal; the dominant ancient pictures of time were the wheel and the downhill slope, and the biblical narrative gave the West its distinctive picture of time as a judged line heading toward a goal. Precision: the claim is narrow. The ancients did imagine some improvement — advances in arts and sciences, a climb from rude beginnings — but the dominant pictures lacked the further idea that history as a whole is a story with a plot, morally judged, headed toward a goal it has not yet reached.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: That confidence still depends on a fixed point above history to say which direction counts as forward — a record of where we have gone cannot supply it — and even committed secularists reach for the biblical arrow’s shape while its source is filed off. Precision: the point here is only historical, and narrower than the moral argument. The claim is that the confidence was born believing in that fixed point and has not obviously found a replacement — not that secular progress is impossible.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the modern idea of progress is, in large part, a biblical inheritance still leaning on the fixed point it was given. That shows where the hope came from. It does NOT, by itself, prove that Christianity is true — a tradition can seed a good idea and still be mistaken about God. The case for the faith’s truth rests elsewhere in this Library, above all on the resurrection. The point is genealogical, not congratulatory.

cards.q: What were the two dominant ancient pictures of time — and what did each make the task of the wise?
cards.a: The wheel (the Stoics’ cosmos repeating exactly, the turn of Fortune) — where nothing is ever finally gained or lost, so the only wisdom is to expect the turn. And the downhill slope (Hesiod’s descent from a Golden to an Iron age) — where the golden age lies behind you, so the task of the wise is not reform but memory: to recover what has been lost, not to build what has never been.

cards.q: What did the Hebrew Scriptures add that the ancient world lacked — and what makes the line a “judged” one?
cards.a: A story that runs in a straight line and is going somewhere — creation, exodus, prophets, a promised kingdom that sets the wrongs of history right. It is judged because it is measured against a standard that lies ahead rather than behind: the prophets do not call Israel back to a golden age but hold up a future in which justice arrives and indict the present for falling short (“let justice roll down like waters”; swords into plowshares).

cards.q: Reply to: “The Greeks and Romans believed in progress too.” Concede what, deny what?
cards.a: Concede it: the ancients did have technical and cultural notions of progress. But that is not the idea being traced. What the dominant ancient pictures lacked is the further conviction — that history as a whole is a story with a plot, morally judged, headed toward a goal it has not yet reached. That load-bearing picture came into the West through the biblical narrative, to which the critic who raised the objection himself gives a central place.

cards.q: Reply to: “This is just Löwith’s secularization thesis, and Blumenberg refuted it.” What narrower claim survives?
cards.a: Concede the strong thesis is contested, and do not lean on it — the rebuttal that progress grows from within history is serious, and this track does not endorse the stronger secularization claim. But the point here is narrower, and it survives: what both sides actually share, and what is not seriously disputed, is that the biblical narrative made a distinctive, load-bearing contribution — time as a line with a moral destination, which the cyclical and declining images did not supply.

cards.q: The Pinker borrowing — which echo carries the weight, and which must NOT?
cards.a: The weight rests on the SINGLE direct echo: Pinker, a thoroughgoing atheist, calls it a “mysterious arc bending toward justice” — Parker’s image and King’s. It must NOT rest on the worn idioms: “swords into plowshares” and “life is sacred” are phrases so worn into ordinary English that little should be made of them on their own. One need not claim Pinker is quoting Scripture unawares — only notice the shape of it.

cards.q: “An arc has to bend toward something.” What does Premise 2 say the hope still needs — and what does it NOT claim?
cards.a: It needs a fixed point standing above history to be measured against: a record of where we have gone cannot, by itself, tell us which direction counts as forward. It does NOT claim that secular progress is impossible — Pinker’s data on declining violence and rising health are real and not disputed — only that the confidence is living on inherited capital and owes an account of the fixed point it still assumes.

cards.q: Reply to: “A secular humanist can just believe in progress on their own terms.” What is conceded, and what is the narrower tension?
cards.a: They can, and many do — the long-run data on declining violence and rising health are real and worth taking seriously; this track disputes not a line of them. The tension is narrower: an arc has to bend toward something, and a measurement of where we have gone cannot say which direction counts as forward. That needs a fixed point above history — which is exactly what the idea was born believing in.

cards.q: Reply to: “Christians were often on the wrong side of the reforms you claim.” What is granted, and what is the point’s actual lane?
cards.a: Granted, without softening it: Christians have repeatedly stood on the wrong side of the very reforms this hope demands, defending what later Christians, reading the same Scriptures, would fight to abolish. But the point is genealogical, not congratulatory. That the source seeded the idea is compatible with those who carried it failing it, often and badly; the claim is that the belief history CAN bend toward justice is an inheritance, not a self-evident fact.

cards.q: What are the two honest limits that keep this whole argument in its lane?
cards.a: First: on its own it is no proof that Christianity is true — that a conviction has biblical roots tells you where it came from, not whether the faith that carried it is right about God. Second: Christians have repeatedly been on the wrong side of the very reforms this hope demands. The point is an inheritance traced, not a trophy claimed; the case for the faith’s truth rests elsewhere, above all on the resurrection.

obj.q: Robert Nisbet showed in his History of the Idea of Progress that antiquity already had real ideas of progress — the Greeks and Romans celebrated advances in the arts and sciences and noted that humanity had climbed from rude beginnings. So the idea of progress is not distinctively biblical at all, and your whole genealogy collapses.
obj.model: Concede it — Nisbet is right about that, and this track says so: the ancients did have technical and cultural notions of progress. But that is not the idea being traced. What the dominant ancient pictures lacked is the further conviction: that history as a whole is a story with a plot, morally judged, headed toward a goal it has not yet reached. That load-bearing picture — a line with a destination, against the images of the cycle and the decline — came into the West through the biblical narrative. Nisbet himself gives that biblical sense of purposive history a central place. So the objection narrows the claim correctly and then misses it: the distinctive contribution is the judged line, not progress as such.

obj.q: This is just Karl Löwith’s secularization thesis dressed up — the modern idea of progress as biblical eschatology in worldly clothes. Hans Blumenberg answered it at length: progress grows from within history, out of the open-ended experience of science and modern self-assertion, not from any borrowed eschatology. The thesis is contested, so your argument is standing on refuted ground.
obj.model: Concede the strong thesis is contested, and do not lean on it: Blumenberg’s rebuttal is serious and this track does not endorse Löwith’s stronger claim. But the point here is narrower, and it survives Blumenberg. What Löwith and Nisbet actually share — and what is not seriously disputed — is that the biblical narrative made a distinctive, load-bearing contribution: time as a line with a moral destination, which the cyclical and declining images did not supply. That narrower, historical claim is enough for everything this argument needs, and it does not require the secularization thesis to be true.

obj.q: You do not need the Bible for any of this. Steven Pinker’s long-run data on declining violence and rising health give a firmer measure of progress than any transcendent standard — the improvement is empirical, you can read it off the tables. Progress stands perfectly well on its own secular terms.
obj.model: They can, and many do — Pinker’s data are real and worth taking seriously; this track disputes not a line of them. The honest tension is narrower. An arc has to bend toward something, and a record of where we have gone cannot by itself tell us which direction counts as forward. For that you need a fixed point above history to measure against — which is exactly what the idea was born believing in. The observation is not that secular progress is impossible, but that it is living on inherited capital, and owes an account of the fixed point it still assumes. So the verdict is bounded, not triumphant: the belief is defensible, but it has not obviously replaced the ground it began with.

obj.q: Even if the hope came from the Bible, so what? A tradition can seed a good idea and still be completely wrong in its central claims. Showing where an idea came from proves nothing about whether its God is real — your genealogy is irrelevant to the truth of Christianity.
obj.model: That is correct, and this track concedes it in our own voice: that a conviction has biblical roots tells you where it came from, not whether the faith that carried it is right about God, and on its own it is no proof that Christianity is true. The case for the faith’s truth is made elsewhere in this Library, resting above all on the resurrection. The argument’s job is narrower and it does not pretend otherwise: to show that the confidence history bends toward justice is an inheritance, not a self-evident fact — an inheritance still leaning on the fixed point it was given. That even confident atheists keep the hope after discarding the God who grounded it is a small thread worth weighing, though never a proof.

unseen.q: If history inevitably bends toward justice, then believing it breeds complacency — why struggle, if the outcome is guaranteed? And worse: treating the present as a necessary rung on the way up lets people tolerate real suffering now as the price of progress. The biblical arrow is a recipe for passivity, not a gift.
unseen.model: That is a real danger, but it is the danger of progress cut loose from any standard above history — not of the hope this essay is tracing. The word “progress” names a movement but not a destination; it says forward without saying toward what, and a century that believed fervently in a guaranteed direction discovered that “forward” can be made to point almost anywhere and can curdle into its own justification. The Christian arc is the opposite of an automatic drift. It is not a smooth upward line: it runs down into suffering before it rises, its clearest emblem a cross before an empty tomb — a road that plumbs the depths before it climbs, and that can be walked with confidence only because the destination is secured by the One who set it there, not because history will arrive on its own. King’s last sermon caught the shape of it: he had “been to the mountaintop,” standing deliberately in the sandals of Moses, shown the promised land from the summit but not himself crossing into it. That is a hope that fuels struggle and refuses to excuse present evil — precisely because the justice it waits for is fixed outside history, not manufactured by it.
